[[Category:Large language model]]
[[Category:Machine learning]]
The '''Chinchilla prescription''' is the compute-optimal division of a fixed training budget between model parameters and training tokens for a Transformer [[large language model (LLM)|language model]], derived by Hoffmann et al. in 2022.<ref>{{#cite:Q3164}}</ref> Its headline result is that the 2 quantities should grow together: every doubling of parameter count should be matched by a doubling of training tokens.


'''Solution via Lagrange multiplier:'''

'''Target'''

Minimise

$$
L(|\theta|,D)=L_{\infty}+\left(\frac{|\theta|_{c}}{|\theta|}\right)^{\alpha_{\theta}}+\left(\frac{D_{c}}{D}\right)^{\alpha_D} \label{eq:loss}
$$

subject to

$$
6|\theta|D-C=0.
$$
(from $\eqref{compute budget}$)

'''Lagrangian and first-order conditions'''

From $\eqref{eq:loss}$

$$
\mathcal{L}(|\theta|,D,\lambda)
=
L_{\infty}+\left(\frac{|\theta|_{c}}{|\theta|}\right)^{\alpha_{\theta}}
+\left(\frac{D_{c}}{D}\right)^{\alpha_D}
+\lambda\,(6|\theta|D-C).
$$

Set all three partials to zero:

$$
\begin{cases}
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial|\theta|}
=
-\frac{\alpha_{\theta}}{|\theta|}\left(\frac{|\theta|_{c}}{|\theta|}\right)^{\alpha_{\theta}}
+\lambda\,6D
=0, & \text{(1)}\\
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial D}
=
-\frac{\alpha_D}{D}\left(\frac{D_{c}}{D}\right)^{\alpha_D}
+\lambda\,6|\theta|
=0, & \text{(2)}\\
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\lambda}
=
6|\theta|D-C=0. & \text{(3)}
\end{cases}
$$

Equation (3) just restates the constraint. Equations (1)–(2) are the substantive conditions.

'''Eliminating $\lambda$'''

From (1):

$$
\lambda=\frac{\alpha_{\theta}}{6|\theta|D}\left(\frac{|\theta|_{c}}{|\theta|}\right)^{\alpha_{\theta}}.
$$

From (2):

$$
\lambda=\frac{\alpha_D}{6|\theta|D}\left(\frac{D_{c}}{D}\right)^{\alpha_D}.
$$

Equate:

$$
\alpha_{\theta}\left(\frac{|\theta|_{c}}{|\theta|}\right)^{\alpha_{\theta}}
=
\alpha_D\left(\frac{D_{c}}{D}\right)^{\alpha_D}
\tag{4}
$$

This is the '''balance condition'''. It is one equation in two unknowns; together with \(6|\theta|D=C\) it pins down \((\theta_{\text{opt}},D_{\text{opt}})\).

'''Solving for the scaling exponents'''

The balance condition is

$$
\alpha_\theta\left(\frac{|\theta|_c}{\theta_\text{opt}}\right)^{\alpha_\theta}
=
\alpha_D\left(\frac{D_c}{D_\text{opt}}\right)^{\alpha_D}.
$$

Divide both sides by $\alpha_D$ and rearrange:

$$
\left(\frac{D_c}{D_\text{opt}}\right)^{\alpha_D}
=
\frac{\alpha_\theta}{\alpha_D}
\left(\frac{|\theta|_c}{\theta_\text{opt}}\right)^{\alpha_\theta}.
$$

Raise both sides to $1/\alpha_D$:

$$
\frac{D_c}{D_\text{opt}}
=
\left(\frac{\alpha_\theta}{\alpha_D}\right)^{1/\alpha_D}
\left(\frac{|\theta|_c}{\theta_\text{opt}}\right)^{\alpha_\theta/\alpha_D}.
$$

Solve for $D_\text{opt}$:

$$
D_\text{opt}
=
D_c
\left(\frac{\alpha_D}{\alpha_\theta}\right)^{1/\alpha_D}
\left(\frac{\theta_\text{opt}}{|\theta|_c}\right)^{\alpha_\theta/\alpha_D}.
$$

Thus

$$
D_\text{opt}\propto\theta_\text{opt}^{\alpha_\theta/\alpha_D}.
$$

Substitute into \(C=6\theta_\text{opt}D_\text{opt}\):

$$
C\propto\theta_\text{opt}^{\,1+\alpha_\theta/\alpha_D}
=\theta_\text{opt}^{\,(\alpha_\theta+\alpha_D)/\alpha_D}.
$$

Invert:

$$
\theta_\text{opt}\propto C^{\alpha_D/(\alpha_\theta+\alpha_D)},\,
D_\text{opt}\propto C^{\alpha_\theta/(\alpha_\theta+\alpha_D)}.
$$

== Compute-optimal allocation ==

The prescription follows from writing the [[language model loss|loss]] as a function of both quantities, with an irreducible floor $L_\infty$ and fitted constants $|\theta|_c$, $D_c$, $\alpha_\theta$, $\alpha_D$,

$$
L(|\theta|,D)
=
L_\infty
+
\left(\frac{|\theta|_c}{|\theta|}\right)^{\alpha_\theta}
+
\left(\frac{D_c}{D}\right)^{\alpha_D},
$$

and minimising it subject to $C = 6|\theta|D$. At the optimum the 2 reducible terms are reduced in balance, and the 2 quantities scale as

$$
\begin{cases}
|\theta|_{\text{opt}} \propto C^{\alpha_D/(\alpha_\theta+\alpha_D)} \\
D_{\text{opt}} \propto C^{\alpha_\theta/(\alpha_\theta+\alpha_D)}
\end{cases}
$$

so the balance between parameters and data is set by the relative size of the 2 exponents. Because $\alpha_\theta$ and $\alpha_D$ are of similar magnitude, both allocation exponents come out near $1/2$, and in practice the prescription reduces to

$$
D \approx 20\,|\theta|,
$$

that is, about 20 training tokens per parameter.

== Contrast with earlier scaling laws ==

Kaplan et al. had recommended spending most of an increased budget on parameters, with $|\theta|_{\text{opt}} \propto C^{0.73}$ and $D_{\text{opt}} \propto C^{0.27}$, and the models built to that advice were correspondingly large and undertrained.<ref>{{#cite:Q3141}}</ref> The Chinchilla result instead grows the 2 in step, which at a fixed compute budget means markedly more data and fewer parameters than the earlier advice implied.

== Worked examples ==

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Allocation for 3 early large language models
! Model
! $|\theta|$
! $D$
! $D/|\theta|$
|-
| Gopher
| $2.8\times10^{11}$
| $3\times10^{11}$
| $1.07$
|-
| GPT-3
| $1.75\times10^{11}$
| $3\times10^{11}$
| $1.71$
|-
| Chinchilla
| $7\times10^{10}$
| $1.4\times10^{12}$
| $20$
|}

Chinchilla was trained on the same compute budget as Gopher, with 4 times fewer parameters and about 5 times more data, and outperformed Gopher, GPT-3, and models several times its size.<ref>{{#cite:Q3164}}</ref> Applied to GPT-3's training budget of about $3.15\times10^{23}$ FLOPs, the prescription gives

$$
|\theta|_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{\frac{C}{120}} \approx 5\times10^{10},
\qquad
D_{\text{opt}} \approx 1\times10^{12},
$$

against GPT-3's actual $1.75\times10^{11}$ parameters and $3\times10^{11}$ tokens.

== Data-constrained regime and the data wall ==

If the available token stock $D_{\max}$ falls short of $D_{\text{opt}}$, the prescription cannot be followed. With $D$ capped, the loss is better described by

$$
L_{\text{data}}(|\theta|, D_{\max})
=
L_\infty
+
\left(\frac{|\theta|_c}{|\theta|}\right)^{\alpha_\theta}
+
\left(\frac{D_c}{D_{\max}}\right)^{\alpha_D},
$$

in which further gains must come from $|\theta|$, from [[algorithmic efficiency]], or from [[synthetic data]], rather than from additional human-written text. This regime is the [[data wall]].

Repeating the tokens already in hand is a partial substitute: up to roughly 4 epochs of repetition costs almost nothing in loss, but beyond that the marginal value of additional compute decays towards zero.<ref>{{#cite:Q3174}}</ref> Estimates of the stock of public human text place its exhaustion, if current trends continue, between 2026 and 2032.<ref>{{#cite:Q3181}}</ref>
